Martin Chemnitz
MAR-tin KEM-nits
proper noun (figure)
Latin Martinus — from Mars, the Roman god of war, thus “of Mars, warlike.” The surname Chemnitz is taken from the Saxon town of that name, itself from a Slavic root meaning “stony brook.”

Biblical Definition

Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586 AD) was the great second-generation Lutheran theologian, so weighty a divine that the proverb ran, “If the second Martin had not come, the first Martin would scarcely have stood” — meaning that without Chemnitz, Luther’s work might not have endured the confusions that followed his death. A man of vast learning who had once thought to give himself to astronomy, Chemnitz was drawn instead into the service of the church, becoming pastor and superintendent at Braunschweig and the chief architect, with Jakob Andreae, of the Formula of Concord (1577), which reconciled the warring Lutheran factions and secured the confessional unity of the Lutheran churches. His most enduring monument is the four-volume Examination of the Council of Trent, a massive, patient, learned dismantling of Rome’s counter-Reformation decrees, in which he answered the canons of Trent point by point from Scripture and the Fathers — a work that served the whole Protestant cause, Reformed as well as Lutheran, against the errors of the papacy. We honor his immense labour, his defence of justification by faith and the sole authority of Scripture, and his services to the truth against Rome. Yet on the Lord’s Supper Chemnitz stood with the Lutherans for the bodily presence of Christ; and here, honoring his labour, we own the Reformed difference plainly, confessing that the believer feeds on Christ by faith through the Spirit, not by any oral eating of His flesh.

Webster 1828 Definition

The “second Martin” of Lutheranism (1522–1586 AD); author of the Examination of the Council of Trent and co-author of the Formula of Concord.

MARTIN CHEMNITZ, proper noun. Latin Martinus (“of Mars, warlike”) + Chemnitz, a Saxon place-name.

German Lutheran theologian (1522–1586 AD); pastor and superintendent at Braunschweig.

Called the “second Martin”; without him, it was said, the first Martin’s work might not have stood.

Chief author of the four-volume Examination of the Council of Trent against Rome’s counter-Reformation.

Co-architect of the Formula of Concord (1577); a Lutheran on the bodily presence in the Supper.

Modern Corruption

A mighty Lutheran defender of the truth against Rome; honored fully, with the Reformed difference owned only on the Supper.

expand to see more

Chemnitz taught no error of the modern kind; the only matter to be named plainly in our voice is the old confessional line dividing Lutheran from Reformed on the Lord’s Supper. Chemnitz was a firm defender of the Lutheran bodily presence, and we honor the seriousness with which he sought to guard the reality of communion with Christ; yet we confess with the Reformed churches that the flesh profiteth nothing where the Spirit is not, and that the faithful truly receive the whole Christ by faith and the Spirit’s working, not by the mouth of the body.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Chemnitz recovers for us is earnest contention for the faith once delivered. His Examination of Trent is a monument of patient, thorough, Scripture-saturated controversy, refusing to let a single false decree of Rome pass unanswered, yet never railing where argument would serve. Against a slothful age that will not read, will not answer error, and will not contend, Chemnitz stands as a rebuke and a model — a workman who fought the good fight of faith with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
